To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

both On- and On-Off direction selective RGCs project robustly to the SC, and that projection-specific differences in On DS RGC physiology are due to differences in the excitatory synaptic input these cells receive.
On-Off and ON DS RGCs both project to the SC, and the two types of cells exhibit projection-specific differences in response properties, somatodendritics morphology, and synaptic input.

On DS RGC subpopulations innervate both the SC and MTN and exhibit projection-specific differences in morphology, excitability, and synaptic input that are consistent with differences in their functional properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms that underlie motion vision and how the brain processes information about object motion.
understanding how the brain processes information about the direction and speed of object motion.
how information about visual motion is encoded in the brain, and the mechanisms by which this information is processed and transformed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
On DS RGC projections are highly specific and that the SC is a major target of On DS RCGs.
On DS RGC axons target either the SC or the MTN.
the brain receives information about direction from On-Off and ON DS RGCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the brain receives information about object motion from several classes of RGCs, which target different retinorecipients, exhibit projection-specific differences in response properties, and are differentially influenced by synaptic input.

the brain receives direction-selective input from a large number of retinal ganglions, and the projection-specific differences in response properties of direction-selective cells are largely attributable to projection-specific differences in excitatory input.
the mouse brain receives information about object motion from a larger number of retinal ganglia cells than previously appreciated.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the visual system uses multiple types of RGCs to provide the brain with information about object motion, and that the visual system is capable of using projection-specific differences in RGC physiology to encode information in different ways.

On-Off and on direction-selective RGCs are both major sources of retinal input to the brain, and that projection-specific differences in retinal input to different brain targets are mediated in part by projection-specific differences in RGC response properties.

the brain receives information about motion in the environment from a larger fraction of RGCs than previously thought, and that the brain receives direction-selective input from a larger fraction and with more specificity than previously thought.
